anf_compare.notes: No ANF or other public-domain English of this homily; translated from the Greek.

bible_refs.note: LXX: τίς ἔστησε τὰ ὄρη σταθμῷ καὶ τὰς νάπας ζυγῷ; Hesychius turns the question into a statement about God.
Exact quotation: Μὴ στήσῃς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ταύτην (Greek word order as Hesychius cites it).

choices.why: Hesychius argues from ἵστημι, which also means to weigh in a balance (Isaiah 40:12 ἔστησεν … σταθμῷ); 'set' keeps the wordplay.
A noun phrase ('an exact weigher') turned into a verb for natural English, with no change of claim.
The pair contrasts stumbles with right actions; plain English words keep the contrast.

choices.english: do not weigh down, on my account
choices.why: ἐξ ἐμοῦ marks Stephen as the occasion; the word play with βεβαρημένους is kept by 'weighed down'.

choices.term: Μὴ ἀναγάγῃς αὐτὴν εἰς τὸν ζυγὸν
choices.english: Do not lift it onto the scale
choices.why: ἀνάγω is to bring up; 'lift onto the scale' is the natural English for putting a weight in the pan.
rejected: Do not bring it up to the scale

pass_a_gloss: [And] this is [it]: for he did not say 'Do not reckon [it] to them', but 'Do not set', surely so that you may learn our Judge to be an exact weigher, weighing for each the deeds in the time of the judgment seat. For if 'he set the mountains in a balance and the glens in a scale', how not much more does he weigh in the balance the things that are ours, whether stumbles or right deeds? 'Do not set to them this sin.' Do not bring it up onto the scale of the judgment; do not weigh down from me those weighed down from themselves; nor let my blessing become for others an occasion of curse, nor my gain a cause of loss to the Jews. §28 I do not wish my sacrifice to become a harm to those sacrificing. For even if … [continues in u02-rem-close]
pass_b_english: …here is the point: he did not say, “Do not count it against them,” but “Do not set it,” surely so that you may learn that our Judge weighs with an exact balance, weighing each person’s deeds at the time of judgment. For if “he set the mountains in a balance and the valleys on a scale” (Isaiah 40:12), how much more does he weigh what is ours, whether our failings or our good deeds?

“Do not set this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). Do not lift it onto the scale of judgment; do not weigh down, on my account, those already weighed down by their own doing; let not my blessing become for others an occasion of curse, nor my gain a cause of loss to the Jews.
I do not want my sacrifice to bring harm on those who offer it. For even if…
source_text:
τοῦτό ἐστιν· οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν· «Μὴ λογίσῃ αὐτοῖς», ἀλλὰ «Μὴ στήσῃς», ἦ πάντως ἵνα
ζυγοστάτην ἀκριβῆ μάθῃς εἶναι τὸν κριτὴν τὸν ἡμέτερον, ἑκάστῳ τὰς πράξεις ἐν τῷ
καιρῷ τοῦ κριτηρίου σταθμίζοντα. Εἰ γὰρ «ἔστησεν τὰ ὄρη σταθμῷ καὶ τὰς νάπας
ζυγῷ», πῶς οὐ πολὺ μᾶλλον ταλαντεύει τὰ ἡμέτερα εἴτε πταίσματα μὲν οὖν εἴτε
κατορθώματα; «Μὴ στήσῃς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ταύτην.» Μὴ ἀναγάγῃς αὐτὴν εἰς
τὸν ζυγὸν τῆς κρίσεως· μὴ βαρήσῃς ἐξ ἐμοῦ τοὺς ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν βεβαρημένους· μηδὲ ἡ
ἐμὴ εὐλογία ἑτέροις γένηται κατάρας ἀφορμή, μὴ τὸ ἐμὸν κέρδος ζημίας τοῖς
Ἰουδαίοις πρόξενον.
28 Οὐ βούλομαι τὴν ἐμὴν θυσίαν βλάβος γενέσθαι τοῖς θύουσιν. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: The section opens mid-sentence: Καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν ('And here is the point') follows the 'And…' that ends the previous section.

Hesychius plays on ἵστημι in Acts 7:60 ('set', also 'weigh in a balance', as in Isaiah 40:12 ἔστησεν … σταθμῷ). 'Set' is kept in both quotations, here and in the previous section, so the wordplay survives.
'Do not count it against them' (Μὴ λογίσῃ αὐτοῖς) is Hesychius's hypothetical alternative wording, not a quotation; it may echo Psalm 32:2 (LXX 31:2) or 2 Corinthians 5:19, so no inline citation.
From 'Do not lift it onto the scale' the words are Hesychius's expansion of Stephen's prayer in Stephen's own voice; the first person continues into the next section.
θύουσιν ('those who offer it') has no expressed object; the sacrifice is Stephen himself. The section ends mid-sentence at Εἰ γὰρ καί.
